text: Okay, so in here there are going to be two relatively large plagioclase grains
towards the center of the field of view. They're low relief, clear, no pleochroism,
but when the polars are crossed you'll see one of them has some nice twinning,
albite twinning, and the other one does not. That's the characteristic of
plagioclase. Sometimes it has twinning and sometimes it doesn't.
Now this is a single large plagioclase crystal and again low relief, clear, kind
of looks like quartz in plain polarized light, but when you cross the polars
then you'll see there is a little bit of twinning on the outer edges but it's
also chemically zoned and so it has this extinction that sweeps from the
interior to the exterior and vice versa. Another example of plagioclase, there's
a single large grain. Again, you can't see it because it's got such low relief
and no pleochroism. When you cross the polars you'll see that part of this
crystal is has lots of twins through it and part of the crystal does not have
twins in it. The inclusions there are quartz and biotite.
Now this one will trick you. So again low relief, no pleochroism. When I cross the
polars you're going to say that looks like quartz and the fact is that that
plagioclase grain in the center does look like quartz. It doesn't seem to have
any twinning, doesn't seem to have any zoning and yet it is plagioclase and I
know it's plagioclase because I spent three hours on an electron probe looking
for quartz in this sample unsuccessfully. This is another example of a large
crystal that has both twinning and zoning so after the polars are crossed you'll
see this kind of trapezoidal feature towards the middle of it with this
sweeping extinction because of the chemical zoning but then there's also
lots of twinning in there. There's some K-Feldspar around the outside and also
little quartz. This is plagioclase from a granite and you'll see once the polars
are crossed that it just has lots and lots of twinning. It's really
characteristic of plagioclase that you see in intrusive rocks. Yeah, there's
some quartz on the edge and I think a little K-Feldspar too.
Now this is one of the most bizarre samples I've ever collected. I think this
was a vesicular basalt and the vesicles were filled with zeolites. Then it was
metamorphosed to amphibolite faces and all the zeolites in that circular
region have been metamorphosed to form plagioclase. Section's a tiny bit thick
so the plagioclase is a little bit yellow but I'm pretty sure that's the
origin of this rather unusual texture.
Now this is plagioclase from a mafic igneous rock and when it's all of those
light-colored laths or the sort of blocky crystals in there across the polars
and you'll see there's twinning, there's some zoning, nice zoning in one of those
crystals, but that kind of simple twinning is really common in volcanic
plagioclase.
Now this is a really bizarre looking plagioclase. It's from an alkali basalt
and it has a lot of melt inclusions in them where they were melt now they're
glass so they're black and when you cross the polars they they stay black but
again you can see the twinning that we see is so characteristic of plagioclase.
Now this last one is a little tricky when I cross the polars you'll see there are
two sets of twins that intersect each other. Plagioclase has two different
twin laws that it follows albite twinning and pericline twinning and this
crystal actually shows both of them. Now this is not the same twinning that you
see in microcline, K-Feldspar, that has a much more noir kind of effect. These
intersect at sharp angles and so they're distinct from K-Feldspar.
